newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britain's Hong Kong Chinese army unit disbanded.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Hong Kong Chinese army unit disbanded.

text.p: The "unsung soldiers" of Britain's only Hong Kong Chinese army unit marched into history on Saturday amid a ceremonial farewell.
The 460 troops watched impassively as their ensign was lowered for the last time at their parade ground on Stonecutters Island in Hong Kong harbour.
Britain shut down the unit, formally part of the British army for 60 years, in preparation for the handover of the colony to Chinese control at midnight on June 30, 1997.
Winter sunshine bathed the parade ground as the Hong Kong Military Service Corps said good-bye with traditional lion and dragon dances and a military parade.
"I feel so miserable. We've been serving Hong Kong for such a long time, you know. I feel a little bit upset to be honest, but we've got no choice," said Warrant Officer So Kam-kei, 38.
The British army first recruited in Hong Kong in 1880 but it was not until 1937 when China was at war with Japan that it began formally employing Hong Kong Chinese servicemen.

In 1941, during World War Two, the Hong Kong Chinese Training Unit was formed. Many of its members were killed or taken prisoner when the Japanese invaded Hong Kong. Some soldiers escaped to China or India and fought on from there.
Not all the troops, described as Hong Kong's unsung soldiers for their vital support role as drivers, cooks, dog-handlers and medical orderlies, entered civilian life on Saturday.
A skeleton staff from the corps will stay on almost to the last moment in support of the British garrison.

"The Hong Kong Military Service Corps will be remembered with honour and with affection, and all who have served in the corps may look back on their work with pride," Hong Kong governor Chris Patten said after inspecting the troops.
Britain has stopped short of translating its gratitude into full British nationality for the servicemen, a source of some discontent.
But it was sadness and regret and not bitterness which marked the day.
"I will miss it very much. I spent half my life serving the British army," said W.Y. Ho, a 31-year-old corporal.
Though many of the soldiers said they would miss military life, none expressed a desire to join the Chinese army.
"No way," said So, "because of the poor pay. I guarantee no-one wishes to join the People's Liberation Army. Most of us will search for another job."
